name: Olga Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Oh, it's a fast day. I buy organic and specialty food for Greenfork Foods in Hallbrook: oat milk, olive oil, grains, small-farm cheeses. I'm up at six, checking overnight supplier messages, and I have an AI assistant draft my first replies and summarise the price lists. Then I'm on calls with growers and co-ops, and twice a week I'm at the cold store checking pallets. I love the growers and the puzzle of it. What wears me out is that the pay is lower than my friends in other firms get, and we run on a mortgage and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful bits are real, but the hype is silly, so don't bet the company on it. At work I'd keep showing the others my prompts. Online I'd be the person who shares the practical tricks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it wouldn't change much for me. The AI saves me maybe an hour a day on admin, and that's it. My real stress is that our savings are tiny and Marek's joinery work goes up and down with the building trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what works, and I'd drop the rest. I'd use the extra hour to build a few more grower relationships, because that's where price breaks come from. And I'd ask Greenfork for a salary review, since I do more than my title says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit like a quiet shift: nothing dramatic, but the bills are still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. If it turns out to be mostly hype, does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Marek's order book thinned this autumn because two housing projects were paused. When he's slow, we eat into the card. So a quiet AI world doesn't mean a quiet household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pressures would you still carry in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the company to share the time the tools save. If I do my admin in half the time, I'd like to spend it on growers or leave an hour earlier for the kids. Otherwise the saving just disappears into more targets.

say: I'd say the useful bits are real, but the **hype** is silly.
I'd share **practical prompts** with colleagues and online.
think: For me it's about an **hour a day** saved on admin, and no more.
Marek's **joinery** work goes up and down, which worries me more than AI.
do: Keep using the tools that **work** and drop the rest.
Use the saved hour on **grower relationships** for better prices.
Ask for a **salary review** because I do more than my title.
feel: **Okay**, like a quiet shift, with the bills still there.
S0.quote: My partner Marek's order book thinned this autumn because two housing projects were paused. When he's slow, we eat into the card.
fieldNote: Home money is **the pressure**, tied to her partner's building trade.
Practical about AI: it saves **an hour**, not more.
Wants **time savings shared**, not turned into targets.

steps.text: Keep the daily AI drafts for supplier emails and price summaries
Use the saved hour to ring two new growers each week
Ask for a salary review at the January appraisal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, let's plan for it. I'd push for a rule that if a company saves money through AI, some of it goes into retraining staff. At work I'd offer to run a lunch session on how to use the tools well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in better shape than some because I already use it daily, but that cuts both ways. If I make my own tasks faster, the boss needs fewer buyers. We're six now; I can see us at three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build myself into the new workflow. I'd write the checks for the automatic reorders, and I'd start offering sourcing advice on the side to two small shops that can't afford a buyer. That could be a few hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit sick at once. I like the change, but I can't pretend the cushion is thick enough to let me take a hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already do some of the tasks listed on that card with AI. What does your team look like in three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who lose are the ones who see this late: the older buyers who don't touch the tools. The people who win are the owners, unless staff and regulators make them share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who benefits, and who loses out, in a world like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say the other four on my team. Two are great with growers but don't trust the tools. I'd try to teach them in the lunch sessions, because I'd rather have them with me than be the one who stayed.

say: I'd say, **plan for it**, and some AI savings should fund retraining.
I'd offer a **lunch session** on using the tools well.
think: I'm in better shape because I use AI daily, but **faster tasks** mean fewer buyers.
We're six buyers now; I can see **three or four**.
do: Write the **checks** for the automatic reorders.
Offer **sourcing advice** to two small shops for a few hundred a month.
feel: **Excited** and a bit sick; the cushion is too thin for a hit.
S1.quote: If I make my own tasks faster, the boss needs fewer buyers. We're six now; I can see us at three or four.
fieldNote: Sees her **own speed** as both a shield and a threat to her team's jobs.
Thinks about **colleagues** who distrust the tools.

steps.text: Write the checks for the automatic reorder rules
Offer sourcing advice to two small shops for a monthly fee
Run two lunch sessions to teach colleagues the tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest story of our lives and we need emergency plans. Support for families, shorter weeks, retraining at public cost. At work I'd stay calm and say we should adapt now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. I'm good with the tools, but if AI does almost any thinking work, then so can a thousand other buyers' assistants. We have no money to wait it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd use my savings, such as they are, to start a small sourcing consultancy for independent shops, using the AI myself. I'd talk to Marek about taking on any work he can, even trade jobs that aren't joinery, and I'd apply for retraining funds the day they open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My heart's going. But also, weirdly, I'm already thinking of what to do, which calms me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very quick. What changes first for you, and what do you do in the first six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd have time to grow slowly and save. With two, I need to be building my own thing before the company does it without me. That means moving now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly desk, with some cold store checking. How do you think about robots coming three years after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots come later, so Marek's trade is safe for a few years longer. That's good, and it makes me think we should keep his business going. Cold store checks I can do for three more years, but the buying itself goes at the start.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest story** of our lives and we need emergency plans.
I'd call for **retraining at public cost** and shorter weeks.
think: If AI does any thinking work, **thousands** of buyers' assistants can too.
We have **no money** to wait it out.
do: Use our little savings to start a **sourcing consultancy** for independent shops.
Ask Marek to take any **trade work** while his joinery is slow.
Apply for **retraining funds** the day they open.
feel: **Alarmed**, heart racing, but already planning, which helps.
S2.quote: With ten years I'd have time to grow slowly and save. With two, I need to be building my own thing before the company does it without me.
fieldNote: Fear turns straight into **action**; she plans while alarmed.
Notes her **partner's trade** lasts about three years longer.
Plans a **consultancy** built on AI itself.

steps.text: Launch a sourcing consultancy for independent shops using AI tools
Build an automated price-comparison sheet for clients
Ask Marek to take any trade work through winter
Apply for retraining funds the day they open

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot for planning. I'd tell friends to start side projects now, and I'd press the government to sort out income support before 2031. At work I'd keep running my lunch sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but optimistic. I can retrain, I'm quick with tools, and Marek's trade lasts longer. The worry is the mortgage, which doesn't care about my optimism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd turn my side work into proper income, aiming for a quarter of my salary by 2028. I'd save for six months of bills, then take a data course in the evenings. I'd also help my team write their own prompts so we move together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but energised. I'd be busy, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What would you do differently in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek and the kids come first. I'd want a fund big enough that a bad six months doesn't wreck us. Then my team, because I'd hate for the older buyers to be pushed out without anyone helping them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you try to help, and who would you try to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sixty-year-old in my team, Ines, hates the tools. I'd sit with her twice a week and show her tricks, because a person who learns the tools in five years keeps her job a bit longer. It's not much, but it's what I can do.

say: I'd say five years is the **sweet spot** for planning and press for income support.
I'd tell friends to **start side projects** now.
think: I'm anxious but **optimistic**; I can retrain and Marek's trade lasts longer.
The **mortgage** doesn't care about my optimism.
do: Grow the side work to a **quarter of my salary** by 2028.
Save **six months** of bills, then take an evening data course.
Help my team write their own **prompts**.
feel: **Anxious** but energised, and busy, which suits me.
S3.quote: The worry is the mortgage, which doesn't care about my optimism.
fieldNote: Optimism is **real but guarded** by money fears, as the mortgage sets the pace.
Wants to **bring colleagues** along, especially older ones.

steps.text: Grow sourcing side work to a quarter of my salary by 2028
Save six months of bills in a separate account
Take an evening data analysis course
Sit with Ines twice a week and teach her tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and we should use it to build a fair system: retraining, fair taxes on the firms that win, and strong unions. I'd tell friends not to treat ten years as forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine, to be honest. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, and I could be running my own small business. Nina will be twenty-two and Tomas nineteen, so they'd be right in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue using AI at work and build the consultancy slowly, aiming to be self-employed within five years. I'd pay down the mortgage and keep a cushion. I'd also join a buyers' network so I'm not alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little guilty, since I know other people have less time and less room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does this still feel urgent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the tools will be like water, so learn what to ask for and how to check. Be curious. Also learn to do something with your hands, because we're told those jobs hold out longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nina and Tomas about work in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still feels worth treating as urgent, just not frightening. I've seen how fast phones changed, and ten years can pass in what feels like two. So I'd keep a plan, not just a mood.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so build a **fair system** with retraining and strong unions.
I'd tell friends **not** to treat ten years as forever.
think: I'd feel **fine**; by 2036 I could run my own small business.
My kids will be **right in it**, at twenty-two and nineteen.
do: Build the **consultancy** slowly and aim to be self-employed within five years.
Pay down the **mortgage** and keep a cushion.
Join a **buyers' network** so I'm not alone.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little guilty about those with less time.
S4.quote: I've seen how fast phones changed, and ten years can pass in what feels like two.
fieldNote: Time reduces fear, but she **refuses complacency** and keeps a written plan.
Aims for **self-employment** within five years, so the plan is about independence, not only safety.

steps.text: Aim to go self-employed with the consultancy within five years
Pay an extra hundred a month off the mortgage
Join a regional buyers' network and meet monthly
Put a little into an index fund every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm fast, but the savings aren't there and the mortgage keeps coming. What would help is retraining funded in advance, a basic income floor, and companies required to share what they save with the people who help them save it. Also a bit of help starting your own thing: small grants, simple paperwork.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think people assume that using AI every day means you're safe. I'm not. I'm only a little further ahead on the same road, and I know it. That's why I try to share what I know with colleagues.

headlineQuote: People assume that using AI every day means you're safe. I'm not. I'm only a little further ahead on the same road, and I know it.
portrait: **Olga Ziegler**, 43, buys organic and specialty food for Greenfork Foods in Hallbrook, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
Her **partner Marek** is a joiner whose orders go up and down; they have two children and a mortgage.
She uses AI **every day**, builds a **side income** early and helps older colleagues learn.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, with fear quickly turning into action.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because savings and the mortgage don't allow a slow start.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining** funded in advance, an income floor, and **small grants** for starting something of her own.
